text:
Sanjay: Quick follow-up on the service-auth RFC — two operational patterns still open: scoped service tokens (token carries project_id & roles) vs single org/service-principal + per-request delegation. Leaning scoped tokens but want a short ops/security checklist before we lock.

Marta: +1 on scoped for least-privilege. main concern is token churn and gateway cache invalidation; we can't hit DB for every request.

Sanjay: Agreed. Draft checklist:
- token format (JWT with `project` + `roles`) and proof-of-rotation
- validation path in gateway (local cache + fallback to authz service)
- rotation/invalidation hooks (KMS + delta stream)
- audit & impersonation headers
- rollout plan + feature flag

Sanjay: example minimal claim set:
```
{
  "sub": "svc:billing-worker",
  "iss": "auth.redwood-inference.internal",
  "project": "proj_12345",
  "roles": ["compute:invoke"],
  "exp": 1710000000
}
```

Alex: Two operational notes:
- audit: make sure token->project mapping is emitted in logs (not full token)
- rotation: short TTL + refresh flow for long-running jobs

Liz: On impersonation: instead of the gateway doing full delegation, have the caller include `x-actor-id` (service that initiated the request) so auditors can see the call chain. We also need an invariant that only the auth service can mint tokens with `act:impersonate` claim.

Kevin: Cache strategy suggestion: gateway keeps an in-memory map token_id -> (project, roles, exp) with 5m TTL and invalidation via auth service notifications. For edge cases, if mapping missing, gateway can hit authz service synchronously but we should track the latency in metrics. Also need rate-limit mapping: token->project => project quota.

Sanjay: Tradeoff: allowing synchronous lookup solves correctness but increases p95 latency. Another option: fallback to an org-level principal if mapping absent. That gives availability but broadens scope — dangerous.

Marta: fallback to broader principal is a privilege escalation vector. If we must support fallback, require a signed `allow_fallback` claim (short-lived) and only allow it for read-only endpoints.

Alex: Agreed. Policy we should enforce in gateway:
1) if token has `project` claim -> validate locally
2) else if `allow_fallback` claim present and endpoint is read-only -> allow
3) else -> reject

Liz: SDK change: clients that mint service tokens should add `x-actor-id` + `x-call-chain` (opt-in) headers and propagate them. That lets observability reconstruct chains without relying on fallback behavior.

Kevin: Suggested rollout: feature flag gate, 20% traffic can use scoped tokens + metrics for cache hit ratio, authz latency, and fallback rate. If fallback > 0.1% -> block rollout.

deploy-bot: deploy status: auth-gateway/main passed CI (build 0d4f3a) :white_check_mark:

Sanjay: Next steps: add an RFC addendum with the checklist above, add a gateway validation PR, and a small auth-service push that emits invalidation events. @Marta volunteers to draft the addendum.

Marta: I'll draft it and ping for review by EOW. :thumbsup: 

Alex: One open question — long-running batch workers: do we issue ephemeral tokens (short-lived + refresh) or long-lived, rotated keys? I prefer short-lived + refresh via client credentials.

Liz: short-lived + refresh + traceable refresh events in audit logs sounds good.

Kevin: I'll sketch the cache invalidation flow and the feature-flag rollout doc.

Sanjay: Thanks all. If nobody objects I'll put the addendum + checklist on the RFC repo and start a canary next week.
